title: Petz Recovery through a Single Polar Transformation for Approximate Quantum Error Correction
abstract: The Petz recovery map provides a near optimal decoder for approximate quantum error correction, but its inverse square-root normalization complicates circuit implementation. We use the polar structure of the Petz recovery isometry to implement recovery through a single quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). We give explicit block-encoding circuits and an extended recovery isometry that yields approximate Petz recovery without postselection. We bound the diamond distance between the approximate and ideal Petz encoding-recovery channels in terms of a spectrum-weighted loss, which provides a channel specific objective for optimizing the QSVT angles. Uniform polynomial approximation yields an asymptotic error bound that decays exponentially with the number of QSVT iterations, at a rate controlled by the smallest nonzero scaled singular value. Applications to Haar-random encoding and the Hayden-Preskill protocol illustrate the tradeoff between circuit depth and recovery accuracy and place existing scrambling decoders within a common Petz recovery framework.
summary: This paper develops a method to implement the near-optimal Petz recovery map for Approximate Quantum Error Correction using a single Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT). By exploiting the polar structure of the map, the authors achieve a circuit-friendly, postselection-free decoder. This work provides a quantifiable measure of performance via the diamond distance, advancing the practical realization of robust quantum error correction.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of implementing the Petz recovery map, a near-optimal decoder for Approximate Quantum Error Correction (AQEC), due to its complex inverse-square-root normalization.
main_result: The authors show that the Petz recovery can be implemented efficiently using a single Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) based on the map's polar structure, yielding an error bound that decays exponentially with the number of iterations.
method: The core method involves reformulating the Petz isometry using its polar structure, which allows the complex recovery map to be realized deterministically via a QSVT sequence.
model_or_system: The study is set within the framework of Quantum Error Correction (QEC), analyzing the relationship between the encoding channel $E$, the Petz recovery map $\mathcal{R}_{	ext{Petz}}$, and the resulting approximate recovery channel $\mathcal{R}_{\vec{	heta}}$.
key_observables: Diamond distance between approximate and ideal channels, Entanglement Fidelity ($F_{	ext{en}}$), and the spectral width derived from singular values.
important_parameters: The error bound depends on the smallest nonzero scaled singular value ($\lambda_{\min}$) and the number of QSVT iterations ($k$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes the encoding environment $\sigma$ is full rank for certain simplifications, and the error bound derivation relies on bounding the diamond distance between isometries.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes detail mathematical derivations involving equations for the Petz map, QSVT transformations, and error bounds.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the Petz map and its limitations, proposes the polar structure approach, derives the QSVT implementation, and finally analyzes the performance using diamond distance bounds and applying the method to specific protocols like Haar-random encoding.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, circuit-implementable method (QSVT) to realize a theoretically optimal decoder (Petz map) for QEC, which is highly relevant for building practical quantum hardware.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Real odd polynomial approximations r(x) to the sign function for k = 4 (blue) and k = 6 (orange) QSVT itera- tions. These polynomials are realized as r(x) = Re[e−iϕp(x)] after a common phase choice. (a) Optimization on [0.2, 1]. (b) Optimization on [0.2, 0.6]. The shaded regions mark the optimization intervals. The black dashed lines mark the tar- get value 1, and the colored dashed lines mark the minimum polynomial values on the respective intervals. Increasing k or restricting the optimization interval improves the approxima- tion.
FIG. 2. Logarithm of the approximation error δ[a,1] as a func- tion of the iteration number k for different values of a. The dashed lines represent the asymptotic expressions in Eq. (52).

FIG. 3. Petz recovery for Haar-random unitary encoding of one logical qubit (nA = 1). Results use a single Haar-random realization for each system size. (a) Ideal Petz entanglement fidelity versus nD −n/2 where n is the number of qubits acted on by U. The black dashed lines mark fidelities 1/4 and 1. (b) Entanglement fidelity of the approximate recovery versus iteration count k for n = 8, nD = 6, using the generic type I block encoding in Eq. (55). The vertical dashed line marks the Grover estimate k∗in Eq. (66).

FIG. 4. Petz recovery in the Hayden–Preskill protocol with one logical qubit (nA = 1) and a Haar-random encoding uni- tary. Results use a single Haar-random realization for each system size. (a) Ideal Petz entanglement fidelity versus the number of output qubits nD. Here n counts the qubits acted on by U, excluding the entangled register B′, which is also available to the decoder. Near-unit fidelity is obtained with only a few qubits in D. (b) Entanglement fidelity versus iter- ation count k for n = 8, nD = 2, using the reduced (II′)-HP block encoding in Eq. (72). One Grover iteration gives a large initial improvement, while the optimized sequences continue toward the Petz benchmark.
